title: Rembrandt's prodigal
hookLine: an old painter paints the father's two different hands on his son's back

lines: A KNEELING SON, ONE SHOE OFF.
AN OLD MAN BENDING OVER HIM.
A BROTHER WHO DOESN'T COME CLOSER.
cards: Most of the canvas is dark. Brown, deep red, shadow. Out of it, light falls on two figures.
A young man kneels with his back to the viewer, his head shaved, one shoe off, the other worn through at the heel. His face is pressed into an old man's chest.
The old man bends over him, eyes half closed, his two hands resting on the young man's back. Off to the right, standing tall in a red cloak, another man watches, and doesn't come closer.
Rembrandt painted this late in his life, art historians think, after years of loss.

teach.h: A GREAT WAY OFF, HIS FATHER RAN.
teach.b: The story is Jesus's, in the fifteenth chapter of Luke. A younger son takes his share of the inheritance, wastes it, ends up feeding pigs and hungry enough to want their food. He walks home with a speech ready.

The King James Bible gives the moment: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the son says a word.
Rembrandt doesn't paint the running. He paints what comes after: the son home, the father holding him.
Now look at the hands. Viewers have noticed they aren't a matching pair. One is broad and strong, the fingers spread, pressing.
The other is slimmer and smoother, resting more gently. Some see a father's hand and a mother's hand.

teach.h: STRENGTH AND TENDERNESS ON ONE BACK.
teach.b: Some see firmness and tenderness together. Rembrandt left no note explaining them, so nobody knows for certain what he meant. And then there's the man in the red cloak.
Viewers take him to be the elder brother, the one who stayed home and did everything right, and who in Luke's story stands outside, angry, refusing to come in.
The father goes out to him too: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." The story ends with the father still speaking. Jesus never says whether the elder brother walked in.
Rembrandt leaves him standing in the light, still deciding.

how: Some Christians meditate on paintings of Bible stories as a form of prayer, looking slowly at one image, and Rembrandt's prodigal son is a picture some return to again and again.

games.why: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." the father runs before the son can give his speech.

practice: Find Rembrandt's Return of the Prodigal Son if you can, or use the picture from the start, and look first at the hands, one strong, one gentle, then let your eye drift to the brother in the red cloak.
Notice which figure your eye keeps returning to, without judging it. If you pray, rest in the line, his father saw him, and had compassion; if not, simply stay with the picture.

wordCard.voice: Rembrandt's prodigal. The Return of the Prodigal Son, painted by Rembrandt late in life: a father's two different hands on his son's back, and an elder brother watching.

orig.note: Greek: to be moved with compassion, felt in the inward parts — "had compassion" in Luke 15:20.

carryVoice: Your line: two hands. One strong, one gentle, on the same back. That's day nine hundred ninety-one.
